paragraph.text: D10. "God gave us dominion over animals"
the meaning of dominion in Genesis is disputed: part of the tradition read it as permission to use animals, and many traditions read it as responsibility and care. Pope Francis's encyclical

itself states that deriving from it an absolute dominion over other creatures is not a correct interpretation of the Bible. Since the text doesn't settle the question on its own, it's worth examining the moral reasons themselves, and many believers reach compassion for animals from their own faith's values.
"It's in Genesis. God made animals for man. Who are you to contradict God?"
In Genesis 1:26-28, God gives human beings dominion over the animals.
Having dominion over something includes the right to use it.
What God authorizes is morally permitted.
So using and eating animals is morally permitted.

The strong version rests on a text that is sacred to millions of people and deserves to be taken seriously. The problem lies in P2: reading "dominion" as unlimited use is disputed within the religious traditions themselves.
fails at P2, and premise P3, being theological, can't be required of those who don't share the same faith.
"God told Peter to kill and eat."
"Do you know better than the Bible?"
"Man is the crown of creation, and the animals were given to him."

Imagine someone leaves you in charge of a garden while they travel. Does being responsible for the garden mean you can pull up all the flowers? No! It means you should take care of it. Many religious people understand that this is what God asked of humans: to take care of animals, not to mistreat them. And anyone, religious or not, can see that making an animal suffer for no reason is wrong.
You can read that dominion the way many religious traditions do: as responsibility, like that of someone looking after something that isn't theirs. Pope Francis, in the encyclical

, wrote that deriving an absolute dominion over other creatures from it isn't a correct interpretation of the Bible. And look at the very next verse (Genesis 1:29): the food given to humans is plants and fruit. It's true that other readers through history have understood dominion as permission to use animals; the text alone doesn't decide between the readings. That's why it's worth looking at the moral reasons themselves too: causing suffering and death without need is something believers and non-believers can assess together, and many believers reach compassion for animals through their own faith's values.
"If God entrusted animals to human beings, how do you think He'd want them treated?"
The argument depends on a specific interpretation of "dominion":
Animals exist for human use, including as food
An important part of the Christian tradition, such as Thomas Aquinas
Human beings care for creation on God's behalf
Many Christian, Jewish and other traditions;
Both readings have support in the text and in history. The argument only works if the first is the only possible one, and it isn't.

text.bold: 1. The text allows more than one reading.

paragraph.text: The verbs in Genesis 1:28 translated as "have dominion" and "subdue" are strong, and major interpreters, such as Thomas Aquinas, concluded that animals exist for human use. But right after the dominion, verse 29 gives humans "every herb bearing seed" and "every tree, in the which is the fruit" as food, and in the Genesis narrative eating meat only appears after the flood. The text alone doesn't force us to read dominion as a license to exploit.

text.bold: 2. The Catholic Church rejects absolute dominion.

paragraph.text: (2015), Pope Francis wrote that deriving an absolute dominion over other creatures from the mandate in Genesis isn't a correct interpretation of the Bible, and linked the idea to "tilling and keeping" in Genesis 2:15.

text.bold: 3. There are religious traditions that defend animals.

paragraph.text: Many Christians, Jews, Buddhists, Hindus, Jains and Seventh-day Adventists practice or recommend vegetarianism for religious reasons. Religion doesn't speak with a single voice.
Even if the text permitted eating animals, it wouldn't require it. A permission doesn't answer whether it's good to do, especially under the conditions of industrial animal farming.

text.bold: 5. In a public debate, the premise has to be shared.

paragraph.text: For those who don't share the faith, "God permits it" isn't a reason. In a debate among people of different beliefs, one has to offer reasons everyone can assess.

text.bold: 6. Moral reasons can be examined on their own.

paragraph.text: already asks: is something good because the gods approve of it, or do they approve of it because it's good? Many theologians answer that God commands what is good for reasons the human conscience can understand. If so, the question "is it right to make an animal suffer and die without need?" can be considered directly, without depending on which reading of a verse prevails. Separating moral analysis from religious authority isn't an attack on faith: it's a way of thinking more carefully about our own actions. And many believers take this path from within their religion, reaching compassion for animals through values their faith already teaches, such as mercy and respect for others. The book of Proverbs (12:10) says that "a righteous man regardeth the life of his beast".

text.bold: 7. Dominion isn't the same as license to do anything.

paragraph.text: Ruling over other beings allows very different forms, from benign paternalism to tyranny, and it's possible to rule over someone and still have duties of justice toward them. The political philosopher Alasdair Cochrane notes that Augustine and Thomas Aquinas didn't take the exclusion of animals from the Bible alone: they inherited much of it from Greek philosophy, above all from the Stoic idea that we have no obligations to those who lack reason (Cochrane, 2010, pp. 17–19). Reading dominion as a license for use owes as much to philosophy as to the text.

text.bold: 8. Reading dominion as a licence carried real weight in history, and that should be said.

paragraph.text: Peter Singer gathers examples from early Christian tradition. Paul, commenting on the law of Moses that forbids muzzling the ox while it treads out the grain (Deuteronomy 25:4), asks whether it is for oxen that God cares, and reads the precept as a lesson for humans (1 Corinthians 9:9-10). Augustine, commenting on the Gospel episodes of the withered fig tree and the drowned swine, concludes that refraining from killing animals and destroying plants is superstition. And Thomas Aquinas, following Aristotle, recognized only sins against God, against oneself and against one's neighbour, none against animals (

, ch. 10). Singer also records more generous minority voices, such as Basil, John Chrysostom and Francis of Assisi, and thinks the biblical text gives little support to reading dominion as stewardship. That assessment is disputed: theologians such as Andrew Linzey, and Pope Francis himself in
, defend the stewardship reading (point 2). The debate confirms point 1: the text doesn't settle the matter alone, and the moral question has to be examined on its own terms (point 6).

text.bold: 9. The problem of evil weighs against reading dominion as a license.

paragraph.text: If God is good, animal suffering is part of the problem of evil, one of the oldest questions in the philosophy of religion: Darwin was already asking, in 1860, why a good God would create wasps that eat caterpillars alive. Anyone who takes this problem seriously already grants that animal pain has moral weight, and causing them avoidable suffering only adds to the evil that faith itself struggles to explain. The page on religious ethics, in Political and ethical objections, covers the subject in more detail.

Faith is an important part of many people's lives, and it's legitimate to seek moral guidance in it. It's also true that biblical texts, at various points, permit eating animals, and that most Christian traditions don't require vegetarianism.

But the tradition itself offers another reading: dominion as care, plant food as the ideal of Eden, mercy toward all creatures. Faced with a text that allows more than one reading, the question that remains is which one fits better with the mercy the tradition itself asks for. And that question can also be answered through the moral reasons themselves, which believers and non-believers can examine together.
